title: Between NPP’s authoritarian agenda and Opposition’s racist battle-plans | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:30
-     - {{hitsCtrl.values.hits}}

“Be afraid. Be very afraid.”

Movie character Veronica Quaife (The Fly)

By Tisaranee Gunasekara

In May 2019, the Hasalaka police arrested 47-year-old M.R. Mazahima, because they couldn’t tell the difference between a ship’s wheel and the Dhammachakka (Wheel of Dhamma). Mazahima was accused of wearing a dress offensive to Buddhist feelings and detained under the ICCRP. The dress was sent to the Department of Buddhist Affairs for identification. 

In July 2025, the Supreme Court ruled that Mazahima’s arrest and detention were wrong and ordered the former OIC of the Hasalaka police to pay her compensation.


If the proposed Organised Crime Prevention Bill goes through, that same police will be given a freehand to arrest any citizen for wearing an ‘organised crime’ kind of dress or tattoo. 

Whoever drafted the Organised Crime Prevention Bill seems to have made liberal use of the cut-and-paste method. For instance, Section 5(2) of Singapore’s Organised Crime Act of 2015, which deals with evidentiary factors for determining the guilt of an accused, states in clause c, “whether that person adopts the style of dress, handsigns, language or tattoos used by known members of the group” (https://sso.agc.gov.sg/Act/OCA2015?ProvIds=P12-.) Section 4(2) of Sri Lanka’s proposed bill, which deals with evidentiary factors for determining the guilt of an accused, states in clause c, “whether the person adopts the style of dress, hand signs, language or tattoos used by known members of organised criminal groups” (https://documents.gov.lk/api/content-file-proxy?file=/bill-content/PL%2015938%20%5BS%5D%20Crime%20Act_1791287837.pdf). Almost word-to-word, including the misspelling handsigns (it should be two words or a hyphenated word).

In some countries organised criminal gangs have an established history of using codes of identification such as tattoos, hand signs, passwords etc. Japan’s Yakuza gang uses elaborate tattoos of dragons and elephants, the Chinese Triads go for dragons and eagles, and Singaporean gangs favour dragons. In 2019, fans and players going to Japan for Rugby World Cup matches were urged to hide some of their tattoos to prevent misunderstandings (https://www.bbc.com/news/newsbeat-49768799). 

What tattoos, hand signals, language, and/or style of dress do Lankan organised crime groups sport? What kind of tattoos, hand signals, language, and/or style of dress would the police be instructed to look out for in a suspect? Or would the police be given a freehand to act according to whatever preconceived notions they harbour? In the absence of clear and specific guidelines, what is to prevent the police from giving into ignorance and prejudices and persecuting citizens (especially young persons with unorthodox appearances), the same way the ICCPR Act was used to persecute Mazahima?

Dreaming of a police State?

In its election manifesto, the NPP promised to reform the Online Safety Act by removing its anti-democratic clauses. That promise is yet to be honoured.

In its election manifesto, the NPP promised to abolish the PTA. That promise was shattered with the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act.

While the NPP Government has not acted repressively so far, it has also taken no steps to reform repressive laws or introduce new laws to broaden and deepen civic freedoms and liberties - as the Sirisena-Wickremesinghe Government did with the 19th Amendment and the Right to Information Act. Instead, the NPP administration is planning to use its supermajority to push through two Bills on terrorism and organised crime which, if enacted in their current forms, will have a deadly effect on the fundamental rights of all Lankan citizens, including JVP leaders and members once they lose power. 

The Organised Crime Prevention Bill was drafted with no public consultation. In consequence, it contains provisions way more draconian and open to abuse than even the Protecting the State from Terrorism Act. For instance, under the PSTA, a suspect can be detained only for 48 hours before being arraigned while under the Organised Crime Prevention Bill, a suspect can be detained for 72 hours before being arraigned.

Imagine what some members of the police would do to a suspect in those 72 hours, especially since the Organised Crime Prevention Bill also allows confessions, if they are made before a police official of or above the rank of assistant superintendent of police (ASP). 

This in a country where the IGP was accused by the AG’s Department of turning police officers into a ‘paramilitary force’ and running “a criminal network, allegedly exploiting police officers under his command for unlawful activities...” That same Deshabandu Tennakoan was a Superintendent of Police (one rank higher than an ASP) when he ordered three suspects to be stripped, thrashed them with a ‘three-wheeler belt’, and forced them to apply Siddhalepa balm on their own genitalia. 

In 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that his conduct was a “stark betrayal of the Rule of Law…entirely repugnant to the virtues of a democratic republic.” In its judgement, the court focused on the systemic nature of custodial torture. “Violations of the kind we have observed in this case are, unfortunately, all too common. These are by no means isolated one-off events but are symptoms of longstanding institutional failures…” The case reveals “a pattern of grave derelictions which has persisted for a considerable period of time” (https://supremecourt.lk/?melsta_doc_download=1&doc_id=44cb0b15-2cbf-48f1-9ff3-7d6b9c4e7caa&filename=sc_107_2011.pdf).

Two fundamental rights judgements made last week remind us that unlawful arrests and custodial abuses are not isolated issues but ‘symptoms of institutional failures,’ as the Supreme Court put it.


On 30 October 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that the Kuliyapitiya police violated the fundamental rights of a jewellery shop owner. The police came into his house on 13 June 2022, accused him of buying gold from a suspect, handcuffed him, made him kneel, and assaulted him in front of his wife and children. They forced him to handover his vehicle and assaulted him some more, demanding gold. CCTV cameras in the shop showed him handing over gold to the officers. When he was eventually produced before a JMO, he was threatened by Inspector Manohara to deny any assault (https://dailyfc.com/supreme-court-slams-police-for-brutal-assault-extortion-orders-compensation-for-fundamental-rights-violations/).

On 30 October 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that the Dompe police violated the fundamental rights of a woman. In October 2019, she went to the police station with a lunch packet for her husband who had been arrested by the STF on allegations of brewing illicit liquor. She too was arrested and assaulted (https://www.dailymirror.lk/breaking-news/Supreme-Court-rules-police-constable-violated-womans-fundamental-rights-through-assault/108-353909).

Less than a week before those judgements, a young suspect died while being held in the Homagama police station. According to the medical report, Ishara Harsha Kumara had suffered multiple injuries including three broken ribs and brain haemorrhage. 

Two days before the custodial death at the Homagama police station, Gampaha Magistrate Bandula Gunaratne requested the Court of Appeal to file contempt charges against the IGP for ignoring a court order. The police had charged a man with possessing drugs, based on false information allegedly provided by officers of the Gampaha Police Anti-Corruption Unit. The Magistrate then ordered the IGP to issue a circular regarding arrests on drug charges. Five months on, the IGP continued to ignore the court order. “If the police treat a court order in this manner, what can be said about everything else in this country?” the Magistrate asked in open court (https://srilankamirror.com/news/gampaha-magistrate-initiates-contempt-of-court-action-against-igp/). 

When guardians of the law turn into serial lawbreakers, it indicates not the presence of a few bad apples but a systemic issue. Instead of understanding the problem and dealing with it, the NPP Government is intent on bringing in a new law which would confer on this same police an unprecedented level of impunity. The police, whose chief officer might face contempt of court charges soon, will soon be able to justify any custodial crime by painting every victim in the lurid colours of an organised criminal.

Early in its tenure, the NPP Government faced a litmus test on its commitment to the rule of law. In February 2025, the Kotahena police shot and killed two suspects arrested for a murder. Many of its supporters thought the Government, as it promised to do, would condemn the action and bring the perpetrators before justice. Instead, the Government indirectly defended this extra-judicial killing. Now the Government is planning to give the police near carte blanche to label any citizen an organised criminal. 

In Kalama Sutta, the Buddha explains to the Kalamas the importance of doing good in this life irrespective of whether they believe in an afterlife or not. This is excellent advice for any Government. Most governments believe they will never lose power. The NPP is no exception. Even so, it would make sense to follow the Buddha’s advice and not enact repressive laws which could and would be used against them in case they lose power, someday.

Racism to the rescue?

Last month, a group of monks led by that self-proclaimed Arhat Umandawe Samanthabadra made a clay figurine of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, stuck poison thorns into it, and consigned it to the custody of folkloric demon Mahasona for punishment. 

Speaking a few days later, President Dissanayake mentioned the incident and wondered about the mentality of those who engage in such practices. 

It is reasonable to assume that none of the monks who engaged in a practice condemned by the Buddha as an animal art believe in Mahasona. The whole sordid spectacle was aimed at inciting supernatural fear in the public mind and using it to weaken the Government. If, for instance, some natural calamity occurs in the coming months, the monks will depict it as supernatural punishment of the Government for jailing Galagoda-Atte Gnanasara. 

Addle Sinhala-Buddhist minds and use the resulting confusion to come to power.

Like Udaya Gammanpila’s baseless diatribe about an evil conspiracy to destroy Ruwanweliseya. 

Remember the Sanda Hiru Seya, built in 2010-2021 between the ancient Dakkina Stupa and Isurumuniya, just two short kilometres from Ruwanweliseya? The massive edifice, an in-your-face symbol of the nexus between rata, jathiya, agama, and the Rajapaksas, was constructed in an archaeologically sensitive area -  and against the advice of the archaeology department. According to former Archaeology Director General Dr Senarath Dissanayake, he asked the then president Mahinda Rajapaksa not to build the edifice in that location or to build a smaller one. His expert advice was ignored and he was compelled to give his permission to the project. 

Where were the patriotic monks and the likes of Udaya Gammanpila when this atrocity was committed? 

The Rajapaksas always used ethno-religious racism to gain/hold power. Ranil Wickremesinghe and Sajith Premadasa, instead of providing a rational oppositional alternative to the toxic Rajapaksa politics, are making their own efforts to appease extremists. Ranil Wickremesinghe was the prime minister and Sajith Premadasa was a key minister when Galagoda-Atte Gnanasara was sentenced to imprisonment in 2018. They, who had no problem with that sentencing then, are now demanding that Anura Kumara Dissanayake pardon the erring monk immediately. In November 2022, President Wickremesinghe said, “No one is entitled to special protection just because they are wearing a robe” (Speech in Parliament - 29 November 2022 https://dbsjeyaraj.com/dbsj/?p=80449). Today former President Wickremesinghe is demanding that all robe-wearers be accorded special protection. 

In the meantime, some robe-wearers are dreaming of becoming an independent political force. In a recent interview, Agalakada Sirisumana thero talked nostalgically about the JHU experiment and opined that the monk-led party could have gained power in 2024 had it endured. He also said that when Galagoda-Atte Gnanasara comes out of prison in four years, “he will be able to provide leadership to this society like a monk-king (Sangha-Raja) with the help of other monks” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=75UD8zUXgok). A Sinhala-Buddhist Iran or Afghanistan.

But to succeed in their combined and separate power projects, lay and robe-wearing politicians need a minority enemy. The JHU rode to parliament on an anti-Christian wave targeting non-Buddhist Sinhalese. The JHU also played an enabling role in the Galagoda-Atte Gnanasara led campaign to create the Muslim enemy in 2012/13. If neither enemy can be resurrected, an effort can be made to revive the Tiger and the Tamil enemy. Udaya Gammanpila has already accused the Government of allowing a Siva Kovil to be built in the Anuradhapura sacred city. A Siva Kovil was indeed built in Anuradhapura, not in 21CE but in 10CE - over 2 millennia ago (https://amazinglanka.com/wp/anuradhapura-siva-kovil/#google_vignette). But to rile up Sinhala-Buddhist fear and anger, any lie, however outrageous would do. 

If the SJB and the UNP fail to oppose the Government on rational, economic, lines, they will soon be overtaken by the Rajapaksas and the robe-wearers who dream of becoming organ-grinders even as they continue to play the customary role of incendiary monkeys.

title: Cost of living crisis: The system destroyer? | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:24
-     - 75

There is nothing to quarrel about the agonising fact that rising cost of living (C-O-L) is a pandemic that has propelled anti-Government protests and street riots right across the Americas, Europe and Asia; and it is this issue that is going to decide the outcome of US Midterm elections.

Ultimate economic thermometer

Many of the protestors and rioters in the EU for example are adolescents who are increasingly concerned about rising price levels, which make college and higher education unaffordable to them. Given the rapid spread of robotic technology and AI in both private and public sectors, the Generation Z’s prospects of gaining employment are becoming increasingly grim. Will these riots and protests ultimately end with a wave of Luddism?  

C-O-L is the ultimate economic thermometer which measures peoples’ happiness or discontent in any economy or society. Prices of consumables rise and fall depending on the stock of supply available in the market. There is no denying that the current pandemic is the consequence of supply constraints driven by two main forces: wars and climate change. The first is recent and the second is much older. But both are beyond the control of monetary authorities and their pet remedy to bring down C-O-L by monitoring the rate of inflation to counter it by raising interest rate and urging Governments to cut public spending is a futile exercise, which will eventually reduce investment, increase unemployment and worsen poverty level.

The post-Cold War economic order, hailed by Fukuyama as  ‘The End of History and The

Last Man,’ ushered in with high hopes for a new era promising lasting economic prosperity and narrowing the wealth gap between rich
and poor nations. The IMF, World Bank and the UN are supposed to be the watchdogs of this order. On the contrary the system so far has produced the most aggressive phase of extractive and finance capitalism since the 1980s, and national Governments are more concerned with the growth and profitability of mega-corporations and financial institutions than with the economic welfare of ordinary households.    

Weaponisation of natural resources and financialisation of the real economy has sacrificed long term economic growth through production of goods and services that promote people’s economic well being but instead is concentrating on short term profits through financial engineering. The market is operating not to satisfy the consumers but to increase the financial returns of corporate shareholders.  It is the share market and not the product market that always captures the news headline. 

Consumers are not to question how and why but to go and buy, and buy what? Whatever the market dishes out through its aggressive marketing techniques. Hedonistic adaptation of consumer tastes and availability of credit facilities has made consumers and especially the young ones to buy what they do not need with money they do not have, perhaps to keep up with the Joneses or to impress someone whom they do not like. In short, the market creates hedonistic wants and sells them as needs.      

In short, Governments have lost control over the market and simply left it to be ruled by financial capitalism. With wars and el-Nino effect supply constraints have pushed up prices of ordinary goods and services and hence the C-O-L crisis.  This crisis cannot be solved by central bank instruments but needs a systemic change.    

The cost-of living crisis is not going to disappear soon but is destined to get worse and may force the long-awaited system change.

Sri Lankan scenario

The AKD/NPP Government came to power with the promise of system change. But so far that change has been confined only to areas of governance and judicial administration. As far as the economy is concerned, the IMF continues to determine the terms and direction of management.  Perhaps the need to bring stability to an economy which was on the brink of bankruptcy and burdened with heavy foreign debt could justify the pragmatic option of going along with the IMF program.  That seemed to have been a popular choice when the Government took control of the Government. As a result, the economy was not only stabilised but even recorded a respectable 4% growth rate last year.  But the pains of that growth had been unequally shared, and it was the lower-income groups that had made the most sacrifice. 

The Government knows very well that the IMF is not a friend of the poor but of the rich and the so-called enterprising. It is these groups that set the prices in the market and ordinary consumers have no choice but to pay or go without buying the products. It is this stratum of society that feels most the pain of increasing C-O-L, and their numbers are swelling.

The Aragalaya generation is part of the global network society that must be closely watching how the C-O-L crisis is developing into a system destroyer by the Generation Z in other parts of the world.  Will the AKD/NPP Government take note of this phenomenon, change its gear and speed up delivering its original promise?

title: South Asia’s demographic shift is an opportunity—but only if the region acts now | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:23
-     - 30

One in five workers worldwide lives in South Asia, where 1.17 billion people are in their prime working years. This represents an enormous economic opportunity. A workforce of this scale can fuel economic growth, create wealth, and drive innovation. South Asia has already reaped some benefits from this demographic dividend: Since 2000, the growing share of working-age adults has contributed to gains in GDP growth and labor productivity.

But this demographic advantage will not last forever. South Asia is aging faster and at lower income levels, than comparable emerging market and developing economies. By 2049, people aged 65 and older are projected to account for 14% of the region’s population, marking the region’s transition from an aging to an aged society.

This shift presents an urgent challenge, but also an opportunity. If South Asia acts now, it can capture more of the economic benefits of its large working-age population while preparing for a future in which more people live longer.

Creating more and better jobs is the first priority

Only 60% of South Asia’s working-age population is employed, while 88% of employed workers hold informal jobs that pay less, offer limited protections and benefits, and make no contributions to the taxes that fund public services. A large working-age population alone cannot deliver a demographic dividend. People need opportunities to put their skills to productive use and they need to remain healthy enough to do so.


That means making it easier for micro, small, and medium enterprises to access finance and grow, streamlining regulations that hold back businesses, and improving education and training so workers have the skills employers need. It also means removing the barriers that keep women from entering and remaining in the workforce, and addressing the rising burden of chronic disease which is a growing issue for working-age people.

The second priority is to prepare for longer lives

Across the region, health systems, long-term care services, pension systems, and labor markets are not equipped for a population that is living longer, but not necessarily healthier. A person born today can expect to live to age 72, but only 61 of those years are expected to be healthy.

Governments can help people remain healthier longer by shifting health systems toward prevention and primary care rather than relying on hospital care. Employers and policymakers can expand mid- and late-career training and create phased pathways to retirement, enabling people to work for as long as they want. And formal long-term care systems, supported by trained and skilled care workers, can improve quality of life for older people while easing the burden on families.

Over time, a healthier older population, supported by the right institutions and opportunities, could generate a second demographic dividend. They could also support a silver economy: Older people are workers, consumers, savers and contributors to their communities. Their needs and preferences can create markets for better housing, health services, care, and financial products. 

Stronger social protection and financial markets will be essential to turning longer lives into greater economic security and opportunity. Only 17% of South Asia’s working-age population contributes to a pension scheme, and just 10% of older South Asians receive pension benefits—the lowest coverage globally. Pension and financial systems need to protect workers’ savings, expand basic coverage for those who need it, and help channel greater savings into productive investment.

A demographic dividend is never guaranteed and the choices South Asia makes now will shape its future. Policies to create more opportunities for young people and support people as they age will better position South Asia to ensure that its demographic transition becomes a source of sustained prosperity.

(The author is the World Bank Vice President for South Asia)

title: Sri Lanka U19 cricketers to make use of MCA experience to win maiden title | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:20
-     - 27

The Sri Lanka Men’s Under19 Asia Cup team shortly before their departure to Oman

The Sri Lanka Under19 cricketers will use their experience of playing in the MCA Premier League to win their maiden Men’s Under19 Asia Cup title when they embarked for Oman on Monday.

Sri Lanka’s Under19 skipper Viran Chamuditha speaking to the media shortly before their departure said, “Playing in the Mercantile tournament has given us a great fillip ahead of the Asia Cup. Virtually everyone in the squad have performed well and I think it will help us make it to the final. We have a well-balanced unit and I am confident that we can do well this time.”

Since 2019 the MCA has opened its doors for Under19 cricketers to perform in their Premier League giving the schoolboys the much needed experience to compete against national cricketers enlisted in the regular line up of top corporate teams.

Sri Lanka has a very unique record in the Men’s Under19 Asia Cup being five-time runners-up in the tournament, and continuing their pursuit of a first title.

The last occasion they ended as runner-up was to India in 2021 and since then they have failed to make it to the final in the last three occasions.

The 13th edition of the 50-over tournament features eight nations with all the matches scheduled to be played at Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Oman.

Sri Lanka placed in Group B alongside Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Malaysia open their campaign on 5 November against Malaysia. Their other matches are on 7 November against Bangladesh and 9 November against Afghanistan. The top two teams from each group will qualify for the semi-finals on 12 November with the final slated for 14 November. 

The squad: Viran Chamuditha (Captain), Senuja Wekunagoda (Vice-Captain), Rehan Peiris, Kithma Withanapathirana, Gimhan Rasanjana, Sanul Weeraratne, Chaniru Senaratne, Lithma Perera, Vigneshwaran Akash, Sethmika Seneviratne, Gimhan Mendis, Lathendra Akash, Himaru Deshan, Stevon Peiris, Kaushika Kumarasinghe. (ST)

title: Almost 8.4m ticket requests for India-Pakistan World Cup tie | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:06
-     - 15

There have been nearly 8.4 million requests for tickets for the group stage match between India and Pakistan at next year’s ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup.

The 2027 edition of the tournament is being co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. The rivals face each other on 10 October at Johannesburg’s Wanderers stadium, which holds just 34,000 spectators.

The same venue is also hosting the final on 21 November, which has resulted in almost eight million ticket applications. The tournament opener on 7 October will be a repeat of the 2023 final which saw Australia stun India in Ahmedabad.

Although India v Pakistan is one of the most highly-anticipated matches in the cricket calendar and the most lucrative financially, it has been a one-sided affair in recent times with India winning their past nine meetings.

Pakistan’s last win against India came in the 2022 Asia Cup. They are in a group with Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier while England join South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and another qualifier. The top three, plus the best fourth-placed finisher, from the two groups progress to the Super 7 stage and from there, the top four teams will qualify for the semi-finals.

Sannasgama Hardware receives the championship trophy at the Melwa Challenge Trophy 2026 Ratnapura District Championship at the Embilipitiya Mahaweli Grounds

The Melwa Group successfully continued its islandwide Melwa Challenge Trophy 2026 cricket tournament with the Ratnapura District Championship, held at the Embilipitiya Mahaweli Grounds, where Sannasgama Hardware emerged as champions, while TNR Balangoda secured the runners-up position. 

The tournament brought together 10 teams, with participants primarily comprising masons, welders and hardware industry representatives, highlighting Melwa’s commitment to strengthening relationships within Sri Lanka’s construction sector through sport. 

The participating teams were Yashoda Hardware Balangoda, TNR Balangoda, Sannasgama Hardware, City Electric Hardware, Faze Ceramic Hardware, Wikrama Hardware, Embilipitiya Stores, Central Hardware, Firoos Hardware Balangoda and Chandana Holding. The Melwa Challenge Trophy 2026 forms part of the company’s broader initiative to recognise the contributions of construction industry professionals while fostering camaraderie, teamwork and stronger industry connections beyond the workplace. With competitions scheduled across several districts, the tournament provides a platform for participants from different regions to showcase their cricketing talent and engage with fellow industry professionals. 

Through this initiative, Melwa continues to reinforce its commitment to the construction sector while establishing a sporting tradition that brings together the people who contribute to Sri Lanka’s infrastructure development.

title: Global tourism arrivals to hit record 1.57 b in 2026, WTM Reports | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:02
-     - 29

Tourism Economics Managing Director EMEA Dave Goodger

International tourist arrivals are forecast to reach a record 1.57 billion in 2026, despite geopolitical tensions, rising travel costs and slower growth, according to the WTM Global Travel Report 2026, released at WTM London.

Produced in partnership with Tourism Economics, an Oxford Economics company, the report projects a 2% increase in international overnight arrivals compared with 2025, while international visitor spending is expected to rise 6 percent to $ 1.8 trillion.

However, global arrivals growth has slowed from 6% in 2025 to just 2% this year, reflecting the impact of conflict in the Middle East, higher airfares and cost-of-living pressures.

“In the face of ongoing disruption, including conflict in the Middle East and rising cost-of-living pressures, the industry is on course for another record year in 2026,” said Tourism Economics Managing Director EMEA Dave Goodger. 

The report highlights a shift toward shorter journeys as travelers adjust their plans in response to higher costs and geopolitical uncertainty.

While international travel between world regions declined by 3% in 2026, short-haul travel increased by the same percentage, particularly within Europe and Sub-Saharan Africa.

Europe recorded a 5% increase in international arrivals, benefiting from travelers choosing destinations closer to home. Africa and Oceania also posted strong growth, with arrivals rising 8% in each region.

Meanwhile, international arrivals to the Middle East fell 40%, reflecting the impact of the conflict involving Iran, which has disrupted air connectivity and weakened long-haul demand.

The report notes that Gulf aviation hubs accounted for 15% of global transit traffic in 2025, underlining the wider effects of the disruption on international travel.

Changing consumer preferences are also reshaping travel demand, with more travelers seeking value for money while continuing to spend on experiences they consider important.

“Leisure travel remains a key priority in consumer budgets, even as travellers are adapting how and where they visit, for example by spending selectively on the experiences that matter most to them or staying closer to home,” Goodger said.

According to the report, one in six travellers selected their most recent international destination primarily for value for money in 2026, compared with around one in 11 in 2025.

At the same time, 56% of surveyed travellers expressed interest in combining budget-conscious choices with premium experiences, indicating opportunities for travel businesses to offer more flexible pricing and services.

The trend toward off-peak travel is also continuing, with 22% of respondents planning to travel at different times of the year than previously, increasingly motivated by better value.

Looking ahead, Tourism Economics expects international arrivals to grow 8% in 2027 if current disruptions ease, with long-haul travel projected to rebound by 11%.

The report forecasts that international arrivals could reach 2.2 billion by 2032, supported by expanding outbound markets, including India and China, and sustained consumer demand for travel.

WTM London Event Director Chris said Carter-Chapman said the findings reflect the theme of this year’s exhibition.

“The key findings of the 2026 report are echoed in the conference theme of this year’s show: ‘Resilience, Rebound and Reinvention: the next era of global travel’,” he said.

title: Vietjet strengthens Sri Lanka–Vietnam connectivity with new Hanoi routes, bookings now open | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 4 November 2026 00:00
-     - 33

Vietjet will launch new services linking Colombo and the Maldives with Hanoi, Vietnam’s capital, further enhancing air connectivity between Sri Lanka and Vietnam while opening up more opportunities for Sri Lankan travellers to explore the world through the airline’s extensive flight network.

The Colombo–Hanoi and Maldives–Hanoi routes, with the latter operated via Colombo, are scheduled to commence operations on 9 February 2027. Each route will operate three round-trip flights per week on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays. Bookings for the new routes are now open. Passengers from Sri Lanka can book Colombo–Maldives flights separately, offering greater flexibility for their travel plans.

Together, these new routes strengthen Vietjet’s presence in South Asia, complementing its existing Colombo–Ho Chi Minh City route, its upcoming Maldives–Ho Chi Minh City service via Colombo, and its extensive network connecting Vietnam with India.

For Sri Lankan visitors arriving in Hanoi, Vietnam’s capital offers an unforgettable introduction to the country. A city where centuries-old heritage meets contemporary energy, Hanoi invites travellers to wander through the atmospheric streets of its Old Quarter, enjoy a leisurely stroll around Hoan Kiem Lake, discover the Temple of Literature and savour its celebrated cuisine. Beyond the capital, travellers can venture to the spectacular landscapes of Ha Long Bay, the majestic mountains of northern Vietnam and the region’s charming traditional villages.

As Vietjet continues to broaden its international network, the airline is bringing the world closer to Vietnam with convenient and affordable connections. A new Da Nang–Jakarta route, launching on December 20, 2026, will operate four round-trip flights per week, further strengthening connectivity across Southeast Asia. Vietjet has also recently launched long-haul services from Hanoi to Almaty, Kazakhstan, and Prague, Czech Republic, opening up new travel opportunities between Vietnam, Central Asia and Europe.

With more flights from Colombo, Sri Lanka travellers can look forward to experiencing the unique charm of Vietnam, discovering new cultures, and creating memorable journeys. Through Vietjet’s growing network, passengers can also enjoy convenient onward connections to a wide range of destinations across Asia, Australia and Europe, making Vietjet an ideal travel partner for exploring the region and beyond
